note: Curated public posts. Plain-English lines are this site's summaries, not the authors' words.

items.plain: Someone counted the new tokens on their own copy of the network: 240 of them, held at 857 addresses, five days after the token rules became final.
items.caveat: A volunteer tally, not an official number.

items.plain: A core developer wants to build a dollar-pegged coin that runs on Kaspa's own rules. Right now it's an announcement. Nothing is built yet.
items.caveat: An announcement. No working product yet.

items.text:
yup. on eth it’s called WETH--an ERC-20 wrapper for ETH. the difference is that all the backing ETH is held under one contract address, while individual WETH balances are tracked in the contract’s storage.

on kaspa, each UTXO simply holds the actual KAS together with the KAS20
items.plain: How tokens differ here: on Ethereum one big contract keeps a list of who owns what. On Kaspa, each coin carries its own token and its own rules, like a banknote with the terms printed on it.

Kaspa Privacy Initiative — Another Exciting Step! 💚🚀

Just yesterday, we demonstrated private KAS payments on Kaspa TN10.

Now we've tested something equally important: what happens if the original operator disappears?

And it worked! 🎉

✅ Original application controller
items.plain: Private payments on Kaspa's test network, and a bonus trick: the payment could still be recovered after the people running the system walked away.
items.caveat: Test network only. Experimental and not audited.

items.text:
PR #31 (KCC-20 Last Call advancement) was merged on October 7, 2026 at 20:38:09 UTC. 14 days from that is October 21. 

KCC-20 is final on October 21.
items.plain: The paperwork math: the token standard entered its last-call period on Oct 7, waited 14 days, and became final on Oct 21.

items.text: Published KIP 22 to help Kaspa users better protect their funds from future quantum attackers by keeping public keys hidden until spending
items.plain: A proposal to keep your wallet's public key hidden until you spend, so a future quantum computer has less to aim at. No network upgrade needed. Wallets would just opt in.
items.caveat: A proposal. It is now an open draft, not a finished standard.

items.text:
tl;dr: It should be better than 'hdd' as-is due to the larger write cache, higher buffer mem and much lower compact freq. It syncs in about 6h on a 5400rpm (cmr) hdd, and is able to maintain steady state under current mainnet conditions. 

At full network load it will be unable
items.plain: A full Kaspa node, the thing that checks every block, synced in about 6 hours on an old-style spinning hard drive. Ten blocks a second on hardware from a junk drawer, at today's traffic.
items.caveat: At today's network load. Heavier load needs faster disks.

items.text: i believe we can get to a stable (and secure) testnet this year
items.plain: Asked whether the big consensus upgrade (DAGKnight) arrives in 2026, a lead developer said he thinks a stable test network is possible this year. Test network. Not the real one.
items.caveat: A hope for a test network. No date for the main network.
